question: A freelance graphic designer realizes a week into a project that the scope discussed with the client is not achievable within the agreed deadline. Which action best reflects managing the commitment in a timely manner?

options.A: Wait until the deadline to explain the delay
options.B: Deliver an incomplete portion of the work
options.C: Extend it without ever asking
options.D: Contact the client now to renegotiate the deadline

explanation: Contacting the client right away to renegotiate the deadline addresses the scope problem while there is still time to adjust the agreement. Waiting until the deadline to explain the delay, delivering only an incomplete portion of the work, and quietly extending the deadline without asking all let the mismatch surface too late or without the client's knowledge.

question: A project team has been hitting every milestone, but energy is fading as the project enters its final, less exciting phase. Which action would most effectively keep the team motivated?

options.A: Connect the remaining tasks to the real impact
options.B: Add several more status meetings
options.C: Assign extra unrelated tasks to keep people occupied
options.D: Extend all deadlines quietly

explanation: Connecting the remaining tasks to the real impact reminds the team why the work still matters even as the exciting parts are behind them. Adding more status meetings and extending deadlines quietly do not address flagging energy, and assigning extra unrelated tasks just to keep people occupied adds busywork instead of purpose.

question: A supervisor at a call center notices that experienced reps have become disengaged even though their performance metrics remain steady. Which action would most effectively re-motivate them?

options.A: Require the reps to submit detailed activity logs
options.B: Give them more autonomy over their methods
options.C: Post their metrics publicly
options.D: Cut their break time short

explanation: Giving experienced reps more autonomy over their methods respects their competence and re-engages people who already meet their metrics. Requiring detailed activity logs and cutting break time short add control and pressure rather than motivation, and posting metrics publicly does not address why steady performers have become disengaged.

question: At Corvale Manufacturing, a production team has met every target for a year, but a new plant manager notices the team seems to be running on autopilot rather than genuine engagement. Which action is most likely to restore real motivation?

options.A: Send a congratulatory email to the whole plant
options.B: Introduce a mandatory point-based competition ranking every shift each week
options.C: Ask each operator what part of the job feels most meaningful
options.D: Increase the production quota for the next quarter

explanation: Asking each operator what part of the job feels most meaningful, then rebuilding schedules around it, treats the autopilot feeling as a signal that the work has stopped connecting to anything the person values. A congratulatory email acknowledges the streak but does not change the day-to-day experience of the job. Increasing the production quota adds pressure without addressing engagement at all. A mandatory point-based competition ranking shifts against each other manufactures short-term intensity but risks turning coworkers against one another rather than rebuilding genuine motivation.

question: Two department heads have been quietly competing for control over a shared budget line, slowing down decisions across both teams. Which action would most effectively overcome this turf war?

options.A: Let the two departments keep competing until one wins
options.B: Clarify shared decision rights upfront
options.C: Cancel the budget line
options.D: Assign one senior executive to arbitrate disputes

explanation: Clarifying shared decision rights upfront removes the ambiguity that is fueling the competition in the first place. Letting the departments keep competing until one wins allows the turf war to continue causing delays, canceling the budget line does not resolve who should control shared resources going forward, and assigning an executive to arbitrate disputes treats each conflict individually instead of preventing them.

question: Two regional sales teams both claim ownership of a shared list of key accounts, and reps from each team have started contacting the same clients independently. Which action would most effectively resolve this turf war?

options.A: Merge the two sales teams
options.B: Remove both team leads from their roles
options.C: Assign each account to one team explicitly
options.D: Let each rep contact whichever accounts they prefer

explanation: Explicitly assigning each account to one team removes the ambiguity that is causing both teams to contact the same clients. Merging the teams and removing both team leads are drastic responses disproportionate to an ownership dispute, and letting each rep contact whichever accounts they prefer leaves the underlying conflict completely unresolved.

question: At Thistledown Media, the design and content departments have been quietly undermining each other's proposals in front of executives for months, each trying to control the direction of new projects. Which action would most effectively overcome this turf war?

options.A: Create a joint project charter defining each team's role
options.B: Ask executives to publicly choose which department is right
options.C: Hold a single mediated meeting and hope the tension resolves itself
options.D: Let both department heads present competing pitches directly to executives

explanation: A joint project charter that spells out each team's role gives both departments a stable, agreed structure to work from instead of relitigating control on every new project. Asking executives to publicly pick a winner escalates the rivalry into a zero-sum contest. A single mediated meeting followed by hoping the tension resolves itself does not create any lasting structure once the meeting ends. Letting both department heads pitch competing proposals to executives every time formalizes the turf war instead of ending it.

question: During a brainstorming session, a team member's idea is not picked, and the team instead moves forward with someone else's plan. Which behavior best reflects effective participation as a team member?

options.A: Stay quiet for the rest of it
options.B: Fully support executing the team's chosen approach
options.C: Bring up the idea again later
options.D: Quietly redo the work using the original idea

explanation: Fully supporting execution of the team's chosen approach shows commitment to the group's decision even after a personal idea was not selected. Staying quiet, bringing the idea up again later, and quietly redoing the work with the original idea all withhold full engagement from the approach the team actually agreed to pursue.

question: A team member consistently attends meetings but rarely offers input unless directly asked. Which change would most improve their participation as a team member?

options.A: Share ideas without being asked
options.B: Attend even more meetings
options.C: Take a few more notes
options.D: Wait until asked before ever sharing an opinion

explanation: Sharing ideas without being asked turns passive attendance into real engagement, which is what participation as a team member requires. Attending more meetings and taking more notes are both still passive, and waiting until asked before ever sharing an opinion is the exact behavior that needs to change.

question: A team lead wants coworkers to adopt a new project-tracking tool that several people are skeptical of. Which approach would most effectively persuade them to try it?

options.A: Mandate the tool company-wide
options.B: Show how the tool solves a problem they already have
options.C: Send a brief one-line memo about it
options.D: List every feature of the tool in detail

explanation: Showing how the tool solves a problem coworkers already have gives them a direct, personal reason to adopt it, which is what persuasion requires. Mandating the tool and sending a brief memo about it both skip explaining any benefit, and listing every feature in detail overwhelms skeptics with information rather than addressing their actual concern.

question: A store manager wants staff to start closing out registers five minutes earlier to reduce nightly overtime costs. Which approach would most effectively persuade them to change?

options.A: Explain accounting detail behind the overtime cost
options.B: Show staff how it protects their hours
options.C: Post a sign near the registers
options.D: Threaten formal write-ups

explanation: Showing staff how closing five minutes early protects their scheduled hours connects the change to something they personally care about, which is what makes persuasion effective. Explaining the accounting detail behind the overtime cost overwhelms staff with information they do not need to act. Posting a sign near the registers is passive and easy to overlook, and threatening formal write-ups relies on compliance through fear rather than genuine buy-in.

question: A product manager at Kestrel Apps wants a skeptical engineering team to prioritize a new accessibility feature over other backlog items for the next sprint. Which approach would most effectively persuade the team to make the change?

options.A: Mandate the change through the sprint planning tool
options.B: Send a company-wide memo announcing the new priority
options.C: Share real user stories showing how the gap blocks people
options.D: List every competitor's accessibility feature in a comparison spreadsheet

explanation: Sharing real user stories that show how the missing feature actually blocks people makes the impact concrete and personal for engineers who build the product. Mandating the change through the planning tool and sending a company-wide memo both announce a decision without giving the team a reason to believe in it. A lengthy competitor comparison spreadsheet supplies information but no human stake in the outcome, so it is far less likely to shift a skeptical team's priorities.

question: A project lead keeps assigning the most visible, high-profile tasks to team members who share their same college background, without realizing it. Which action would best help overcome this bias?

options.A: Continue assigning tasks by gut feeling
options.B: Ask for volunteers each time
options.C: Track assignments and review the pattern regularly
options.D: Assign tasks alphabetically

explanation: Tracking task assignments and reviewing the pattern regularly turns an unconscious habit into something visible that can actually be corrected. Continuing to assign by gut feeling is the exact behavior producing the bias, asking for volunteers each time still lets the same confident, similar people opt in repeatedly, and assigning tasks alphabetically ignores skill and interest entirely rather than addressing the bias in who gets chosen.

question: A manager writing performance reviews notices she consistently rates employees who work similar hours to her own as 'highly dedicated,' regardless of actual output. Which action would best help overcome this bias?

options.A: Base ratings on documented output data
options.B: Write reviews faster
options.C: Continue rating on perceived dedication
options.D: Ask other managers if they share her impressions

explanation: Basing ratings on documented output data replaces the manager's unconscious hours-based impression with an objective measure that is not tied to how similar an employee's schedule looks to her own. Writing reviews faster does not touch the underlying bias, continuing to rate on perceived dedication is the bias itself, and informally asking other managers whether they share her impressions could just as easily confirm a shared bias rather than correct it.

performanceIndicator: Recognize and respond to ethical dilemmas
question: A junior buyer discovers that a preferred vendor has been quietly overbilling the company by small amounts for months, and no one else appears to have noticed. Which response best reflects recognizing and responding to this ethical dilemma?

options.A: Say nothing since the amounts are too small to matter
options.B: Confront the vendor loudly
options.C: Quietly switch to a new vendor
options.D: Report the overbilling to a supervisor

explanation: Reporting the overbilling to a supervisor ensures the issue is addressed through the proper channel, even though the amounts are small. Saying nothing because the amounts seem too small to matter dismisses a real ethical problem, confronting the vendor loudly bypasses internal reporting and can escalate the situation unnecessarily, and quietly switching vendors avoids the problem without ever raising it internally.

performanceIndicator: Recognize and respond to ethical dilemmas
question: A coworker asks a new employee to log two extra hours on a shared timesheet that were never actually worked, framing it as 'no big deal since everyone does it.' Which response best reflects recognizing and responding to this ethical dilemma?

options.A: Log the two extra hours anyway
options.B: Ask the coworker to stop this practice
options.C: Feel uneasy about it, but comply
options.D: Decline and honestly log only the hours worked

explanation: Declining the request and honestly logging only the hours actually worked keeps the timesheet accurate regardless of what others may be doing. Logging the extra hours goes along with the falsification, feeling uneasy but complying anyway still results in a false timesheet, and asking the coworker to stop this practice addresses the request in general but does not by itself correct this employee's own entry.

question: A customer service rep receives a call from a client who is upset after a shipment arrived three weeks late and interrupted an important event. Which response best demonstrates empathy?

options.A: Immediately offer a refund without addressing concern
options.B: Explain the shipping policy in detail
options.C: Transfer the call quickly
options.D: Restate the concern in her own words

explanation: Restating the client's concern in her own words shows the rep genuinely heard what went wrong before moving to a solution. Immediately offering a refund without addressing the concern skips acknowledging the client's frustration, explaining shipping policy in detail focuses on procedure instead of the client's experience, and transferring the call quickly avoids engaging with the concern altogether.

performanceIndicator: Treat others with dignity and respect
question: During a team meeting, a junior employee proposes an idea that a senior colleague privately believes is flawed. Which response best reflects treating the junior employee with dignity and respect?

options.A: Say nothing at all and move on
options.B: Dismiss the idea immediately in front of the group
options.C: Interrupt loudly to correct it
options.D: Ask questions to explore the idea's merit

explanation: Asking questions to explore the idea's merit treats the junior employee's contribution as worth engaging with, even if the senior colleague has doubts. Saying nothing and moving on and interrupting loudly to correct it both fail to give the idea a fair hearing, and dismissing it immediately in front of the group is the most direct disrespect to the person who spoke up.

performanceIndicator: Treat others with dignity and respect
question: At Ferncliff Logistics, a warehouse supervisor learns that an employee with a noticeable speech impediment has been repeatedly passed over for a training opportunity because a coworker finds the way he communicates 'unprofessional.' Which action best reflects treating the employee with dignity and respect?

options.A: Ask the coworker to quietly document more examples first
options.B: Assign him to the training based on his qualifications
options.C: Move the employee to a role with less customer interaction
options.D: Hold a mandatory diversity training session for the entire warehouse team next month

explanation: Assigning him to the training based on his qualifications directly corrects the unfair decision and treats his communication style as irrelevant to whether he has earned the opportunity. Asking the coworker to document more examples first treats the coworker's bias as a legitimate starting point rather than addressing it. Moving the employee to a role with less customer interaction punishes him for a coworker's prejudice instead of correcting it. A mandatory diversity training session for the whole team may be useful longer term, but it does nothing to fix this specific missed opportunity.

question: Two warehouse associates argue loudly over who gets to use the only forklift first, each insisting their task is more urgent. Which action best reflects using conflict-resolution skills to address this?

options.A: Let them keep arguing loudly until one walks away
options.B: Help them agree on a fair order to use it
options.C: Flip a coin to decide
options.D: Report both associates to a supervisor

explanation: Helping them agree on a fair order to use the forklift resolves the actual disagreement over urgency. Flipping a coin decides randomly without addressing whose task is genuinely more urgent, reporting both associates to a supervisor escalates a solvable disagreement instead of resolving it, and letting them keep arguing loudly until one walks away leaves the underlying conflict completely unresolved.

question: A five-person product team cannot agree on which of three feature ideas to build next, and the debate has stalled for two meetings in a row. Which action would most effectively help the team reach consensus?

options.A: Let the debate continue until people give up objecting
options.B: Cancel the project
options.C: Rank the ideas by shared criteria
options.D: Assign the decision to the most senior member

explanation: Ranking the ideas by criteria the whole team shares gives everyone an objective, common basis to converge on one option, which is what building consensus requires. Canceling the project avoids the decision entirely, assigning it to the most senior member skips the team's input rather than building agreement among them, and letting the debate continue until people give up objecting produces silence rather than genuine consensus.

question: A nonprofit board is split evenly between two venue options for its annual fundraiser, and the disagreement has become personal between two board members. Which action would most effectively help the board reach consensus?

options.A: Pick the cheaper venue automatically
options.B: Let the two members debate it privately and decide
options.C: Cancel the fundraiser entirely
options.D: List shared criteria and vote as a full board

explanation: Listing criteria the whole board shares and then voting as a full board gives every member a voice in a structured decision, which is what building consensus requires. Picking the cheaper venue automatically ignores the board's actual disagreement, canceling the fundraiser entirely avoids the decision rather than resolving it, and letting the two members debate privately and decide leaves the rest of the board out of a decision that affects everyone.

question: A department director has the authority to approve expense reports and notices one submitted by a close friend on the team. Which action best reflects using power appropriately?

options.A: Deny it automatically to avoid favoritism
options.B: Review it by the same standard
options.C: Ask a colleague to review it instead
options.D: Approve it faster since a trusted friend submitted it

explanation: Reviewing the report by the same standard used for everyone else uses the director's approval authority fairly regardless of the personal relationship. Denying it automatically overcorrects by punishing the friend for a relationship that has nothing to do with the report's validity, asking a colleague to review it instead avoids exercising the director's own responsibility, and approving it faster because a trusted friend submitted it lets the friendship influence an official decision.

question: A plant manager at Rourke Industries has the authority to assign overtime shifts, which come with extra pay. She has been quietly assigning most of the extra shifts to a nephew who also works on the floor. A new HR director reviewing scheduling records notices the pattern. Which action best reflects using power appropriately going forward?

options.A: Rotate overtime shifts using a documented, published schedule
options.B: Continue the current informal assignment process
options.C: Ask the nephew to voluntarily decline future overtime shifts on his own
options.D: Quietly reduce the nephew's shifts without changing the process

explanation: Rotating overtime shifts through a documented, published schedule replaces personal discretion with a transparent process that treats every eligible employee the same way, which is what appropriate use of power looks like going forward. Continuing the current informal process leaves the same favoritism-prone system in place. Quietly reducing the nephew's shifts without changing the process fixes one symptom while leaving the manager's unchecked discretion intact. Asking the nephew to voluntarily decline future shifts puts the correction in the hands of the person who benefited from the favoritism rather than fixing how shifts are actually assigned.

performanceIndicator: Use social media to solicit ideas
question: A small bakery owner wants fresh ideas for new seasonal menu items from her regular customers. Which use of social media would most effectively solicit their ideas?

options.A: Post daily bakery photos
options.B: Ask followers to comment their ideas
options.C: Share a poll of existing menu items
options.D: Post a long history of the bakery's founding story

explanation: Asking followers to comment their ideas directly invites new suggestions in a way customers can respond to immediately. Posting daily bakery photos and sharing the bakery's founding story are one-way content that does not ask for anything back, and a poll of existing menu items only gathers opinions on what's already offered, not new ideas.

performanceIndicator: Use social media to solicit ideas
question: A community theater wants suggestions from its social media followers for which play to produce next season. Which post would most effectively solicit those ideas?

options.A: Post the season schedule
options.B: Share a post about last season's ticket sales
options.C: Ask followers which play they want
options.D: Reposting a review from last year

explanation: Asking followers which play they want directly invites the specific input the theater is looking for. Posting the season schedule and reposting a review from last year share information rather than requesting any response, and a post about last season's ticket sales reports past results instead of asking what to produce next.

performanceIndicator: Use social media to solicit ideas
question: Meridian Coffee Roasters wants to crowdsource ideas for a new limited-edition drink from its most engaged social media followers before the holiday season. Which approach would most effectively solicit usable ideas from them?

options.A: Post a professional video celebrating last year's drink
options.B: Run an open comment thread asking for drink ideas
options.C: Share a poll ranking three drinks the team already designed
options.D: Repost customer photos and captions from last year's holiday drink launch

explanation: Running an open comment thread that directly asks for drink ideas invites followers to contribute their own suggestions in a format built for responses. A professional video celebrating last year's drink and reposting customer photos from last year's launch both look backward and ask nothing of the audience. A poll ranking three drinks the team already designed only gathers a preference among options the company picked itself, rather than soliciting new ideas from followers.

question: A startup's operations manager needs to see which project tasks depend on others and how a delay in one task will push back the finish date. Which project-management tool should she use?

options.A: A daily task checklist
options.B: A work breakdown structure of all tasks
options.C: A Kanban board showing each task's current status
options.D: A critical path diagram

explanation: A critical path diagram maps task dependencies and shows how a delay in one task pushes back the project's finish date, which is exactly the information the manager needs. A checklist, a work breakdown structure, and a Kanban board all organize tasks, but none of them shows how delays in one task affect the overall schedule.

question: A construction startup wants to estimate how long a new task will realistically take by combining optimistic, most likely, and pessimistic time estimates into one weighted figure. Which project-management tool produces that estimate?

options.A: A Gantt chart of task start and end dates
options.B: A PERT time estimate blending three duration guesses
options.C: A simple daily task checklist
options.D: A basic Kanban status board

explanation: A PERT estimate blends optimistic, most likely, and pessimistic time guesses into one weighted duration, which is exactly the calculation the startup wants. A Gantt chart schedules tasks along a timeline, a task checklist just lists work items, and a Kanban board tracks status, but none of them compute a weighted time estimate.

question: A software startup's three developers are each assigned to two overlapping projects, and the project manager notices two projects are competing for the same developer during the same week. Which project-management technique should she apply to resolve the conflict?

options.A: Critical path analysis to find which tasks drive the schedule
options.B: A responsibility assignment matrix mapping each team member's deliverables
options.C: A Gantt chart of both projects' timelines
options.D: Resource leveling to reschedule tasks around the conflict

explanation: Resource leveling adjusts the project schedule so that a team member is not double-booked across two projects in the same week, which directly solves the conflict the project manager is facing. Critical path analysis identifies which sequence of tasks controls a single project's total duration, but it does not resolve competition for a shared resource across two projects. A responsibility assignment matrix clarifies who owns which deliverable, not when they will have the time to do it. A Gantt chart displays each project's timeline but does nothing to reschedule tasks around a resource conflict.

performanceIndicator: Calculate cost of goods sold from beginning/ending inventory
question: Bristle & Bloom Décor began the year with $22,000 in inventory, purchased $85,000 of merchandise during the year, and ended the year with $19,000 in inventory. What was its cost of goods sold for the year?

options.A: $63,000, cost of goods sold for the year
options.B: $85,000, cost of goods sold for the year
options.C: $88,000, cost of goods sold for the fiscal year
options.D: $107,000, cost of goods sold for the year

explanation: Cost of goods sold equals beginning inventory plus purchases minus ending inventory: $22,000 + $85,000 − $19,000 = $88,000. The other figures come from leaving out one of the three amounts in that calculation, such as omitting the ending inventory or using only the purchases total.

question: GreenLeaf Meal Co. spent $8,400 on digital marketing last month and acquired 60 new customers. What was its customer acquisition cost (CAC)?

options.A: $140, customer acquisition cost for the month
options.B: $8,400 total, customer acquisition cost for the month
options.C: $70, customer acquisition cost for the month
options.D: $210, customer acquisition cost for the month

explanation: CAC equals marketing spend divided by new customers acquired: $8,400 ÷ 60 = $140. The other figures come from common mistakes such as not dividing by the customer count, dividing by half the spend, or dividing by the wrong customer count.

question: A subscription coffee company spent $12,000 on paid social ads and $3,000 on a referral program last month, gaining 100 new customers combined from both channels. What was the company's blended customer acquisition cost per new customer?

options.A: $120, blended customer acquisition cost per new customer
options.B: $30, blended customer acquisition cost per new customer
options.C: $214, blended customer acquisition cost per new customer
options.D: $150, the company's blended customer acquisition cost per new customer

explanation: Blended CAC is total acquisition spend across all channels divided by total new customers, regardless of which channel they came from: ($12,000 + $3,000) ÷ 100 = $150. $120 comes from counting only the paid-social spend and ignoring the referral program's cost. $30 comes from counting only the referral spend and ignoring paid social. $214 comes from dividing the total spend by a subset of the new customers instead of the full 100.

performanceIndicator: Calculate customer lifetime value (CLV) and the LTV:CAC ratio
question: A pet-supply subscription box earns $25 in gross margin from each order and the average customer places 8 orders before cancelling. If it costs $50 to acquire each customer, what is the LTV:CAC ratio?

options.A: 3 to 1, LTV:CAC ratio
options.B: 6.4 to 1, LTV:CAC ratio for this subscription box
options.C: 4 to 1, LTV:CAC ratio
options.D: 2 to 1, LTV:CAC ratio

explanation: CLV is gross margin per order times the number of orders before cancellation: $25 × 8 = $200, and dividing by the $50 acquisition cost gives an LTV:CAC ratio of 4 to 1. The other ratios come from using the wrong margin, order count, or acquisition cost in that calculation.

performanceIndicator: Calculate customer lifetime value (CLV) and the LTV:CAC ratio
question: A DTC skincare brand calculates an LTV:CAC ratio of 1.5 to 1 for last quarter. What does this ratio indicate about the brand's customer economics?

options.A: The ratio clears the typical benchmark, so the acquisition spending looks justified
options.B: The ratio shows acquisition cost exceeds lifetime value for this cohort
options.C: The ratio means the brand recovers its cost within one month of signup
options.D: The ratio is below the healthy benchmark, signaling weak customer economics

explanation: An LTV:CAC ratio of 1.5 to 1 falls short of the roughly 3-to-1 benchmark investors use to judge sustainable acquisition spending, so it signals weak customer economics rather than a comfortable margin. Reading the ratio as clearing the benchmark reverses what a below-benchmark number means. Saying acquisition cost exceeds lifetime value misreads the ratio: at 1.5 to 1, lifetime value is still greater than acquisition cost, just not by enough. Recovering cost within one month describes a payback period, a different metric than the LTV:CAC ratio.

question: Falcon Auto Parts had cost of goods sold of $280,000 last year and average inventory of $40,000. What was its inventory turnover rate?

options.A: 7.0 inventory turns per year, company-wide
options.B: 4.0 inventory turns per year
options.C: 9.0 inventory turns per year
options.D: 5.0 inventory turns per year

explanation: Inventory turnover equals cost of goods sold divided by average inventory: $280,000 ÷ $40,000 = 7.0 turns per year. The other figures come from using a different inventory or cost figure than the ones given in the problem.

question: Boutique A holds an average of $80,000 in inventory and posts $560,000 in annual cost of goods sold. Boutique B holds an average of $40,000 in inventory and posts $200,000 in annual cost of goods sold. Which statement correctly compares their inventory turnover rates?

options.A: Boutique A cycles inventory faster, turning it about seven times yearly
options.B: Boutique B turns inventory faster, since a smaller balance signals quicker cycling
options.C: The two boutiques cycle inventory at similar rates overall
options.D: Boutique A cycles inventory slower, holding twice Boutique B's inventory

explanation: Turnover equals cost of goods sold divided by average inventory: Boutique A's $560,000 ÷ $80,000 = 7.0 times a year, versus Boutique B's $200,000 ÷ $40,000 = 5.0 times, so Boutique A cycles inventory faster despite carrying a larger inventory balance. A smaller average balance alone does not guarantee faster turnover; it depends on the sales volume moving through it, which is what makes Boutique B's superficially smaller balance misleading. The two turnover rates are not equal, and Boutique A is not the slower of the pair — it is the faster one.

performanceIndicator: Calculate unit economics (contribution per unit after variable costs)
question: Harbor Roastery sells its coffee for $16 per unit, with variable costs of $6.25 for beans and $2.75 for packaging and shipping. What is the contribution per unit?

options.A: $4.00, contribution per unit
options.B: $9.75, contribution per unit before packaging
options.C: $13.25, contribution per unit
options.D: $7.00, contribution per unit for this bag of coffee

explanation: Contribution per unit equals selling price minus variable costs: $16.00 − $6.25 − $2.75 = $7.00. The other figures come from leaving out or misapplying one of the two variable cost components in that subtraction.

question: A new hire at a print shop wants to use the industrial cutter for the first time. According to standard equipment policy, what must happen before she operates it?

options.A: She may begin once a supervisor is nearby
options.B: She can start now since the cutter has a safety guard
options.C: She should watch a coworker demonstrate it first
options.D: She must complete required training first

explanation: Standard equipment policy requires completing the required training before operating machinery like an industrial cutter, regardless of supervisor presence. Being supervised, having a safety guard installed, or watching a coworker once are all reasonable-sounding steps, but none of them substitute for the formal training and sign-off the policy requires.

question: An employee notices that a forklift's brake pedal feels spongy during her shift. What does equipment policy require her to do?

options.A: Finish the shift, then mention it at the end
options.B: Tag it out of service and report the defect right away
options.C: Keep using it carefully since it still stops
options.D: Ask a coworker to test the brake instead

explanation: Equipment policy requires tagging out a forklift with a suspected brake problem and reporting it immediately, since an unsafe machine should not stay in use. Finishing the shift first, continuing to use it because it still stops, or having a coworker test it instead all leave a potentially unsafe forklift in operation, which the policy does not allow.

question: A warehouse's equipment policy requires a documented pre-shift inspection checklist for every powered pallet jack before use. A supervisor is short-staffed and tells an operator to skip today's checklist since the jack "was fine yesterday." What should the operator do?

options.A: Skip the checklist since the supervisor said it was fine yesterday
options.B: Fill out the checklist from memory without inspecting the jack
options.C: Politely decline and complete the checklist before operating the jack
options.D: Operate the jack as instructed, since it has run without any issue all week long

explanation: Company equipment policy requires the pre-shift checklist regardless of how the jack performed the day before, so the operator should decline the shortcut and complete it before use. A supervisor's informal authorization does not override a documented safety policy. Filling out the checklist from memory without actually inspecting the jack defeats its purpose since nothing was actually checked. A jack running without issue all week is not the same as a completed inspection for today's shift, since a defect can develop at any time.

question: Before the operations team can begin fulfilling a new product line, they need updated specs from the design department. What is the most effective way for the operations manager to coordinate this handoff?

options.A: Set a firm deadline with design for the specs
options.B: Wait for design to send specs on their own timeline
options.C: Assume the specs will arrive soon
options.D: Start production using last year's specs

explanation: Coordinating a handoff between departments works best when the receiving team sets a clear deadline for what it needs, rather than leaving the timing open. Waiting for design to send specs on its own schedule risks delaying operations with no accountability. Assuming the specs will simply arrive is not coordination at all, and starting production on outdated specs risks building the wrong product.

question: Which federal agency sets and enforces workplace health and safety regulations for most private-sector employers in the United States?

options.A: The Federal Trade Commission
options.B: The Occupational Safety and Health Administration
options.C: The Department of Labor's wage division
options.D: The Environmental Protection Agency

explanation: OSHA, part of the U.S. Department of Labor, is the federal agency that sets and enforces workplace health and safety standards for most private employers. The FTC regulates competition and consumer protection, a labor department's wage division handles pay and hour rules rather than safety, and the EPA regulates environmental impacts, not workplace safety.

question: Under OSHA regulations, what must most employers with more than ten employees do regarding workplace injuries?

options.A: Report every minor cut to OSHA directly
options.B: Post injury logs on the company website
options.C: Keep a yearly log of recordable workplace injuries
options.D: File a report with the local police department

explanation: OSHA requires most employers with more than ten employees to maintain a yearly log of recordable workplace injuries and illnesses, not to report every minor incident individually. Posting injury logs publicly is not a general OSHA requirement, and workplace injuries are handled through OSHA recordkeeping, not by filing a police report.

question: A small manufacturing company has 18 employees and experienced a workplace injury that required more than first aid. Under OSHA recordkeeping rules, what must the company do?

options.A: Report the injury to OSHA if the employee ends up missing more than 30 days
options.B: Log the injury once it results in lost work time
options.C: Record the injury on the OSHA 300 log, since it exceeds first aid
options.D: Skip the OSHA log since companies under 20 employees are exempt from recordkeeping

explanation: OSHA recordkeeping rules require logging on the OSHA 300 log any work-related injury that is more than a minor first-aid case, regardless of the employee's specific lost-work-day count or the company's size at 18 employees. Tying the requirement to a 30-day absence threshold describes a different OSHA provision, not the basic recordability standard. Waiting until the injury causes lost work time ignores that a beyond-first-aid injury is already recordable. The small-employer partial exemption applies only to certain low-hazard industries with ten or fewer employees, not to this 18-employee manufacturer.

question: A warehouse supervisor discovers that mislabeling a batch of returned goods as "new" would let the company resell them at full price. What is the ethical response?

options.A: Relabel the goods as new since customers won't notice
options.B: Label the goods as returned, even at a lower price
options.C: Discard the goods instead of reselling them
options.D: Ask a manager to decide informally

explanation: The ethical response is to label the returned goods accurately even though it means selling them for less, since misrepresenting their condition deceives customers for profit. Assuming customers won't notice the difference doesn't make the mislabeling honest, it just makes it harder to catch. Discarding usable returned goods is unnecessarily wasteful when accurate labeling and a lower price are enough, and leaving the decision to an informal conversation sidesteps setting a clear, honest policy.

question: An operations manager receives an offer from a supplier: a personal cash bonus if she directs all future orders to that supplier without comparing bids. What should she do?

options.A: Accept the bonus quietly
options.B: Split the bonus with her team
options.C: Decline the bonus and keep using normal bidding
options.D: Take the bonus but still compare bids

explanation: The ethical response is to decline the bonus and keep choosing suppliers through the normal, unbiased bidding process, since accepting payment tied to steering business is a kickback. Accepting the bonus quietly is the clearest ethics violation, and splitting it with the team spreads the same wrongdoing rather than fixing it. Taking the bonus while still comparing bids does not solve the conflict of interest the bonus itself creates.

question: A project team finished a new website redesign two weeks late but under budget. When evaluating the project's results, what should the team examine besides the budget outcome?

options.A: Whether the client invoice matched the contract
options.B: Whether the deliverable met its original quality
options.C: How the team felt about the pace
options.D: Whether marketing liked how the launch was announced

explanation: Evaluating a project means checking whether the final deliverable met its original quality and scope, not just whether it came in under budget. An accurate invoice is a bookkeeping detail, not a measure of project success. How the team felt about the pace is worth knowing but does not evaluate the deliverable itself, and marketing's opinion of how the launch was announced is a separate matter from whether this website redesign met its goals.

question: A project's final report shows it hit 9 of 10 planned milestones on schedule. What does this best indicate about the project's execution?

options.A: Strong execution against the original plan
options.B: The project manager under-promised on scope
options.C: The team consistently underestimated milestone timing
options.D: The client will likely renew the contract

explanation: Hitting 9 of 10 milestones on schedule is a direct sign of strong execution against the plan the project was built around. It does not by itself tell you whether the manager set the scope too low, and consistently missing time estimates would show up as late milestones, not on-schedule ones. Whether the client renews the contract depends on factors well beyond this one project's milestone record.

question: A six-month software project came in on time and under budget, but user adoption after launch is only 20 percent of the target the sponsor set. How should the project team evaluate this outcome?

options.A: As an unqualified success, since it hit both its schedule and budget targets
options.B: As a project that hit its delivery targets but missed the business outcome intended
options.C: As a failure, since adoption missed its target
options.D: As inconclusive, since adoption metrics rarely reflect project quality

explanation: The project met its own schedule and budget targets but fell well short of the adoption level the sponsor actually needed, so the fair evaluation is that it succeeded on delivery but failed on business outcome. Calling it an unqualified success ignores that schedule and budget are only two of several measures of a project's real value. Calling it an outright failure ignores that the team did meet its delivery commitments. Dismissing adoption as an unreliable metric isn't supported here — a 20 percent result against a stated target is a specific, meaningful shortfall, not statistical noise.

question: A project finished two days early. On its own, why is this NOT enough to call the project a success?

options.A: Early finishes usually mean rushed work
options.B: Finishing early typically raises total cost
options.C: It doesn't show whether quality or scope were met
options.D: Meeting the schedule proves budget and scope were fine

explanation: Finishing early says nothing about whether the deliverable actually met its quality or scope requirements, which is why schedule performance alone can't confirm success. Early finishes don't reliably signal rushed work any more than they reliably signal careful work — the pace alone doesn't tell you. Finishing early doesn't typically raise total project cost either. And hitting the schedule is not proof that budget and scope were also handled well; each dimension has to be checked on its own.

question: A project's post-launch review shows the product met every scope requirement and passed all quality tests, but the launch happened three weeks behind schedule. Was the project a success?

options.A: Partially, since scope and quality were met
options.B: No, since missing schedule means the project failed
options.C: Yes, entirely, since the delay doesn't matter
options.D: No, deadlines matter most

explanation: The project is a partial success: it met every scope requirement and passed all quality tests, even though it missed the original schedule. Treating any missed element, including the schedule, as an automatic total failure ignores that scope and quality were both fully met. Saying the delay doesn't matter at all ignores that missing the schedule is still a real shortfall worth noting. And while deadlines matter, this review shows they are not the only measure of the project's outcome.

question: Two similar store-renovation projects wrapped up last quarter. Project X finished on time, on budget, and customer foot traffic rose 15 percent afterward. Project Y finished two weeks late and 8 percent over budget, but foot traffic rose 40 percent afterward. Which project should be judged more successful overall?

options.A: Project X, since finishing on time and on budget are strong success signals
options.B: Project X, since it is the safer choice for future planning
options.C: Project Y, since its stronger business result outweighs its overruns
options.D: Neither, since a fair comparison needs more financial detail

explanation: Project Y's much larger 40 percent lift in foot traffic is the more meaningful business result, and it outweighs a two-week delay and a modest budget overrun, so Y is the more successful project overall. Treating on-time, on-budget delivery as automatically the strongest success signal ignores that the actual business outcome — the reason the renovation was undertaken — favors Y by a wide margin. Calling Project X the 'safer' choice doesn't address which project actually performed better. And while more financial detail is always welcome, the foot-traffic gap here is large enough to judge the two projects without it.

question: A print shop's ink supplier has delivered every order on time for the past year, but ink quality has quietly declined, causing more printing defects each month. What does this vendor's performance record show?

options.A: On-time delivery doesn't guarantee quality
options.B: The supplier's reliability outweighs quality here
options.C: The defects likely trace to shop presses
options.D: The vendor relationship should end now

explanation: A vendor's on-time delivery record says nothing about product quality, so a supplier can be perfectly reliable on schedule while its quality quietly erodes — exactly what's happening here. Treating shipping reliability as an excuse for a real quality decline ignores that the two are separate performance dimensions, both worth tracking. Blaming the shop's own presses isn't supported by anything in the scenario, which describes a change in the ink itself. And ending the relationship immediately skips evaluating whether the issue can be resolved first.

question: A packaging vendor has held pricing steady for two years and responds to emails within a day, but its on-time delivery rate has slipped from 98 percent to 81 percent over the last two quarters, causing repeated production delays. How should the buyer weigh this vendor's overall performance?

options.A: As stable, since pricing and communication have not changed
options.B: As declining, since delivery reliability is now disrupting production
options.C: As improving, since responsiveness remains strong
options.D: As unchanged, since a two-quarter dip in one metric is normal seasonal variation

explanation: A delivery rate that has fallen from 98 to 81 percent, and is already causing production delays, is a material decline in the vendor's core performance, so the fair reading is that overall performance is declining despite steady pricing and responsive communication. Calling the vendor stable overlooks that on-time delivery — the metric most directly tied to production — has moved sharply in the wrong direction. Calling it improving conflates fast email responses with actual delivery performance, which is worsening. And dismissing a two-quarter, 17-point drop as normal variation that will self-correct isn't supported by anything in the scenario; a change this size and duration is a real signal, not noise.

question: During a shift at a commercial bakery, an employee's sleeve catches fire briefly on a stovetop burner and she suffers a minor burn on her forearm. According to standard accident procedure, what should happen immediately after the burn is treated with first aid?

options.A: Wait until the end of the shift to mention it to anyone
options.B: Post a handwritten warning sign near the stovetop so other kitchen staff notice it
options.C: Document the incident and notify a supervisor
options.D: Have the employee finish her shift before filing any paperwork

explanation: Standard accident procedure calls for documenting the incident and notifying a supervisor right after first aid is given, regardless of how minor the burn seems, so there's a record and the hazard can be assessed. Waiting until the end of the shift to mention it delays both the documentation and any needed follow-up. Posting an informal handwritten warning sign is not a substitute for the formal incident report and supervisor notification the procedure requires. And finishing the shift before filing paperwork just delays the same required step rather than replacing it.

question: Which of these is an example of a FIXED operating cost for a small retail store?

options.A: Monthly rent for the storefront
options.B: Hourly wages for part-time cashiers
options.C: The cost of packaging materials used for each purchase
options.D: Credit-card processing fees

explanation: Rent for the storefront stays the same regardless of how much the store sells each month, which is what makes it a fixed cost. Hourly wages for part-time cashiers, packaging materials, and credit-card processing fees all rise and fall with sales volume or staffing needs, making them variable costs instead.

question: Which of these is an example of a VARIABLE operating cost for a food truck?

options.A: The cost of ingredients used for each meal sold
options.B: The truck's monthly loan payment
options.C: Annual liability insurance
options.D: The annual vendor permit fee

explanation: Ingredient costs rise and fall directly with how many meals are sold, which makes them a variable cost. The truck's loan payment, its liability insurance, and its vendor permit fee are all paid on a fixed schedule regardless of how many meals are sold.

question: A boutique's operating costs rose 20 percent last quarter even though it sold roughly the same number of items as the prior quarter. Which explanation is most consistent with that pattern?

options.A: A variable cost, like packaging, must have driven the increase since sales volume
options.B: The store simply recorded fewer total costs than before
options.C: A fixed cost, like rent or a lease payment, increased regardless of sales
options.D: Sales volume increased even though total unit counts appear flat

explanation: Since unit sales stayed roughly flat, a cost that scales with each sale wouldn't explain a 20 percent jump — that points instead to a fixed cost, like rent or a lease payment, rising independent of sales volume. Blaming a variable cost like packaging contradicts the flat sales figure, since variable costs move with volume, not against it. The scenario describes costs rising, not the store recording fewer costs, so that option misreads the situation. And the problem states unit sales stayed flat, so an increase in sales volume isn't supported by the numbers given.

question: A dental office stores patients' health records and payment information in a cloud system. Which practice best protects that data's confidentiality?

options.A: Print the records for a backup file
options.B: Share the login credentials with every staff member
options.C: Store the records on a single shared computer
options.D: Encrypt records, require role-based login

explanation: Encrypting stored records and limiting access by role are the concrete technical and administrative controls that protect confidential health and payment data. A paper backup doesn't protect the digital records and creates its own security risk. Sharing login credentials broadly defeats the purpose of individual access controls, and storing everything on a single shared computer with no access limits leaves the data open to anyone who uses that machine.

question: An employee wants to check customer order details from her personal phone while off the clock. Which security precaution best protects confidentiality here?

options.A: Let her use the office Wi-Fi password
options.B: Allow it as long as she promises not to forward it
options.C: Ask her to memorize details instead of writing
options.D: Require a company VPN and multi-factor login

explanation: A company VPN combined with multi-factor login gives verified, controlled access to customer data from a personal device, which is what confidentiality requires here. Sharing the office Wi-Fi password doesn't verify who is connecting or secure the data in transit. A promise not to forward or screenshot information relies on trust rather than an actual technical control. And asking her to memorize details instead of writing them down doesn't address the real risk, which is unsecured access from an unmanaged device.

question: What is the best definition of project management?

options.A: Planning and overseeing resources toward a goal
options.B: Handling the day's routine tasks
options.C: Managing a company's full-time staff
options.D: Tracking a department's yearly budget

explanation: Project management is the planning and overseeing of resources — people, time, money, materials — toward completing a specific goal, not simply keeping up with routine daily work. Handling the day's routine tasks describes ordinary operations, not managing a project. Managing full-time staff describes general people management, and tracking a yearly budget describes financial oversight; neither captures the planning and coordination that defines project management.

question: A team has just finished defining the project's goals, budget, and timeline. Which project management phase comes next?

options.A: Closing the project and archiving final files
options.B: Restarting the planning phase
options.C: Executing the planned work
options.D: Reporting results to stakeholders

explanation: Once goals, budget, and timeline are defined, the project moves into the execution phase, where the planned work actually gets carried out. Closing and archiving happens at the very end, after the work is complete, not right after planning. Restarting planning would only make sense if the plan itself needed revision, which isn't indicated here, and reporting results to stakeholders typically happens during and after execution, not in place of it.

question: A project is in its execution phase when the client requests a significant scope change midway through. What does sound project management practice call for?

options.A: Refuse any change once execution has begun
options.B: Accept the change immediately since keeping the client happy outweighs the schedule
options.C: Quietly absorb the extra work without telling the client
options.D: Formally evaluate the change's impact on schedule and cost before agreeing

explanation: Sound project management calls for formally evaluating how a scope change affects schedule and cost before committing to it, so the team and client both understand the tradeoffs. Refusing any change outright ignores that scope changes are sometimes necessary and can be managed with the right process. Accepting immediately without evaluating the impact risks blowing the schedule or budget without anyone realizing it until it's too late. And absorbing the extra work quietly hides the real cost of the change from the client, which undermines the trust the relationship depends on.

question: What is the primary purpose of a business's purchasing function?

options.A: Acquiring goods and services a business needs
options.B: Managing the company's payroll system
options.C: Setting product prices
options.D: Negotiating the lowest price on every single item

explanation: Purchasing exists to acquire the goods and services a business needs to operate, from raw materials to office supplies. Chasing the lowest price on every single item while ignoring quality or delivery terms describes a narrow, risky purchasing tactic, not the function's actual purpose. Managing payroll is a human resources function, and setting product prices is a pricing or marketing decision, neither of which is what purchasing does.

question: A hardware store's purchasing manager needs to decide how much lumber to reorder this week. Which factor should most directly guide that decision?

options.A: The store's overall annual revenue
options.B: The staff's weekly work schedules
options.C: The supplier's marketing materials
options.D: Current inventory levels versus expected demand

explanation: The most direct driver of a reorder decision is how current inventory compares with expected demand — too little risks stockouts, too much ties up cash. Overall annual revenue is too broad a figure to guide a single reorder decision, staff schedules affect who can receive and shelve the lumber but not how much is needed, and a supplier's own marketing materials describe what they're selling, not what the store actually needs.

question: A manufacturer's purchasing department always buys from the supplier offering the lowest unit price, without evaluating delivery reliability or quality history. Lately, production has been delayed repeatedly by late and defective shipments. What does this reveal about the department's purchasing approach?

options.A: It has minimized the company's material costs
options.B: It weighs price too heavily against other supplier factors
options.C: It reflects a sound total-cost-of-ownership approach to sourcing
options.D: It shows the department is prioritizing short-term savings over supplier reliability

explanation: Repeated delays and defects from a supplier chosen purely on unit price show that price is being weighed too heavily against reliability and quality, the other factors purchasing needs to consider. Calling the approach a cost-minimization success ignores the real cost of production delays and defective shipments, which erase any savings on the unit price. It is the opposite of a sound total-cost-of-ownership approach, which would factor in exactly the reliability and quality problems this department is now experiencing. And the outcome — repeated production delays — shows the tradeoff is actively hurting the business, not correctly prioritizing it.

question: A bakery switches to a flour supplier that consistently delivers on the scheduled morning delivery window instead of at random times throughout the day. What is the most likely effect on the bakery's productivity?

options.A: Bakers start on schedule, less idle waiting
options.B: Productivity likely stays about the same regardless
options.C: Ingredient costs will fall regardless of timing
options.D: Customer traffic will increase

explanation: Bakers can begin production right when ingredients arrive on a predictable schedule, cutting the idle time they'd otherwise spend waiting on a random delivery. Delivery timing does affect production, since bakers can't start baking until the flour is actually in the building. Ingredient costs are a separate matter from delivery timing and wouldn't automatically fall, and there's nothing in the scenario connecting delivery reliability to customer traffic.

question: A boutique's purchasing team keeps running out of a popular fabric mid-season because they only reorder once the shelves are already empty. What is the productivity impact of this reordering habit?

options.A: Fabric quality steadily improves each season
options.B: Production stalls whenever the fabric runs out
options.C: Store foot traffic declines each month
options.D: None, since production substitutes another fabric fast

explanation: Once the fabric actually runs out, cutting and sewing on that line has to stop until more arrives, so production stalls exactly when the shelves go empty — the direct productivity cost of reordering only after stock hits zero. Fabric quality has nothing to do with a reordering schedule, and store foot traffic is a sales metric, not a production one. And substituting a similar fabric on short notice isn't guaranteed or free of delay — sourcing, cutting patterns, and dyeing often differ enough that a swap takes real time.

question: A furniture manufacturer's purchasing department switches from a supplier with a two-week lead time to one offering the same parts with a five-day lead time, at a slightly higher unit cost. After the switch, the assembly line's average downtime waiting on parts drops sharply. How should this outcome be explained?

options.A: The shorter lead time let production keep a smaller buffer, cutting downtime
options.B: The higher unit cost signals a better-quality part that assembles faster on the line
options.C: Downtime dropped for reasons unrelated to the supplier switch
options.D: The new supplier's pricing structure directly caused the productivity gain

explanation: Cutting lead time from two weeks to five days lets the assembly line hold a smaller, more responsive parts buffer and still avoid running out, which directly reduces the waiting that caused downtime — the shorter lead time, not the price, is what changed. A higher unit price doesn't by itself indicate a faster-assembling part; nothing in the scenario describes any change to the part's design or fit. Attributing the drop to unrelated reasons ignores that it happened right after the supplier switch, which is a real, identifiable cause. And it's the shorter lead time that reduced downtime, not the pricing structure itself, which only affects unit cost.

question: A retail stockroom holds high-value electronics. Which security precaution most directly reduces the risk of internal theft?

options.A: Post a 'no shoplifting' sign at the entrance
options.B: Require two employees during stock counts
options.C: Install brighter lighting in the parking lot
options.D: Rely on employees to self-report missing stock counts

explanation: Requiring two employees present during stock counts creates built-in oversight that directly discourages and catches internal theft of high-value electronics. A shoplifting sign is aimed at customers, not employees, and doesn't address internal theft at all. Brighter parking-lot lighting is a general safety measure with no direct connection to what happens inside the stockroom. And relying on employees to self-report missing inventory puts the check in the hands of the very people who would need to be honest about their own theft, which isn't a real safeguard.

question: A small office stores employee personnel files in an unlocked filing cabinet in an open area. What security precaution addresses this risk most directly?

options.A: Ask employees to be careful around the cabinet
options.B: Post a sign asking visitors not to touch it
options.C: Move the files to a locked, restricted-access cabinet
options.D: Hire additional office staff

explanation: Moving personnel files to a locked cabinet in a restricted-access room directly closes the specific gap described — unlocked files in an open area — by controlling both physical access and who is allowed near them. Asking employees to be careful is not an actual control and relies on informal vigilance. A sign asking visitors not to touch the cabinet does nothing to stop anyone who ignores it. And hiring more staff doesn't address unauthorized access to the files at all.

question: Which best describes the sequence connecting a product's raw materials to the finished item in a customer's hands?

options.A: The company's internal accounting ledger
options.B: The marketing plan for a new product launch
options.C: A single supplier's price list
options.D: The linked suppliers that move a product to customers

explanation: The network of linked suppliers, manufacturers, and distributors that moves a product from raw material to the customer is what 'supply chain' describes. An accounting ledger tracks financial transactions, not the physical movement of goods. A marketing plan describes how a launch will be promoted, and a single supplier's price list is just one small piece of pricing information within a much larger chain.

question: A toy company sources components from a single overseas factory. When a storm shuts down that factory's port for a month, the company's entire production line halts. What weakness in the company's supply chain does this reveal?

options.A: Excess inventory sitting unused based on inflated seasonal forecasts
options.B: An overreliance on a single supplier, with no backup if that source is disrupted
options.C: A pricing dispute between the company and its factory
options.D: A shortage of demand for the company's toys

explanation: Sourcing every component from a single overseas factory with no backup means one localized disruption — a storm closing one port — can halt the entire production line, which is exactly the overreliance the scenario reveals. The problem isn't excess inventory sitting unused; the halt happened because inputs stopped arriving, not because of a warehouse backlog. Nothing in the scenario describes a pricing disagreement with the factory, and a production halt caused by a supply disruption is the opposite of a demand shortage — demand isn't described as the issue here at all.

question: A furniture maker shares its production forecast with its lumber supplier each month so the supplier can plan its own output. What does this practice best illustrate?

options.A: A one-time favor for a supplier the maker tends to like
options.B: Supply-chain partners planning via shared data
options.C: A legal requirement for furniture manufacturers
options.D: A pricing negotiation tactic

explanation: Sharing production forecasts so a supplier can plan its own output is a textbook example of supply-chain partners coordinating through shared information for mutual benefit. It isn't a one-time favor; it's an ongoing planning practice both sides rely on. Nothing requires furniture manufacturers to share forecasts by law, and sharing a production forecast is about planning coordination, not a pricing negotiation.

question: Two companies in the same supply chain jointly fund a shared warehouse near a port to cut both of their shipping costs. What does this best illustrate?

options.A: A merger combining both companies' entire operations
options.B: A one-sided cost-cutting move by one company
options.C: Collaboration between supply-chain partners
options.D: An antitrust violation

explanation: Jointly funding shared infrastructure like a warehouse to lower costs for both companies is a form of collaborative investment between supply-chain partners, not a full merger. A merger would combine the companies' entire operations under one management structure, which isn't what's described here. It isn't one-sided either, since both companies fund and benefit from the warehouse. And sharing warehouse costs to cut shipping expenses is a common, legal form of supply-chain cooperation, not an antitrust violation.

question: Two competing snack brands that both distribute through the same regional grocery chain begin sharing real-time shelf-inventory data with each other to jointly reduce out-of-stock incidents across their category. A retail analyst calls this arrangement risky. What is the most likely reason for that concern?

options.A: The data-sharing system might crash
options.B: Competitors coordinating this closely could drift into coordinating on pricing
options.C: Sharing data between direct competitors raises antitrust concerns
options.D: The grocery chain might not approve of the arrangement

explanation: Direct competitors sharing granular operational data like real-time inventory raises antitrust and collusion concerns, since that kind of close coordination can be a first step toward coordinating on pricing or output, which regulators scrutinize closely — that's the real risk an analyst would flag. A system crash is a technical concern, not the legal and competitive one the scenario is pointing to. The concern named is specifically about the two competitors coordinating with each other, not about whether the retailer approves of the arrangement.

question: Before operating a table saw for the first time, what safety precaution should an employee follow?

options.A: Ask a coworker whether the saw seems fine today
options.B: Wear safety glasses and use the blade guard
options.C: Adjust the blade to a safe cutting height
options.D: Skip the guard for better visibility

explanation: Standard safety precaution before using a table saw is wearing safety glasses and keeping the blade guard in place, protecting against flying debris and accidental contact with the blade. Casually asking a coworker whether the saw 'seems fine' is not a real safety check. Adjusting blade height is a normal setup step but isn't itself a safety precaution, and removing the guard for visibility defeats its entire purpose.

question: A warehouse employee is asked to lift a heavy box from a low shelf. What safety precaution should she follow?

options.A: Ask a coworker to watch her lift it
options.B: Bend her knees and lift with her legs
options.C: Estimate the box's weight, then request help if needed
options.D: Lift it as quickly as possible

explanation: Bending the knees and lifting with the legs rather than the back is the standard precaution for lifting a heavy box safely, protecting against back injury. Simply having a coworker watch isn't a safety measure, it's just observation. Estimating the weight and requesting help if needed is good practice, but it addresses a different risk — an especially heavy load — not the basic lifting technique for this box. And lifting quickly increases injury risk rather than reducing it.

question: A maintenance worker at a manufacturing plant needs to service a conveyor belt that is normally guarded by an interlocked safety cover. The interlock has been malfunctioning for a week, and a supervisor tells him to just reach around the cover carefully since a full repair will take days. What should the worker do?

options.A: Follow lockout/tagout procedures to de-energize the belt first
options.B: Report the interlock issue but proceed carefully as told
options.C: Reach around the cover carefully as instructed, since a quick repair seems low-risk
options.D: Wait for the interlock to be fixed

explanation: A malfunctioning interlock on a conveyor guard is exactly the situation lockout/tagout procedures exist for: fully de-energizing the belt before anyone services it, regardless of how long a full repair will take. Reporting the issue is good, but continuing to work near the belt without de-energizing it still leaves the worker exposed to the hazard the guard was meant to prevent. Reaching around the cover 'carefully' assumes a moving or energized belt poses no real risk if the worker is cautious, which is not a safe assumption around unguarded machinery. And simply waiting for the interlock to be fixed does nothing to let the necessary maintenance happen safely in the meantime — the belt still needs proper lockout/tagout to be serviced at all.

question: A small fire breaks out in a trash can in the break room. What is the first thing an employee should do?

options.A: Activate the fire alarm
options.B: Try to put it out alone
options.C: Take a photo of the fire to document it for later
options.D: Ask a coworker what they think should happen

explanation: The first step in a workplace fire, even a small one, is activating the fire alarm so the building's emergency response begins immediately. Trying to extinguish it alone first risks injury and delays the alarm if the fire grows. Stopping to photograph the fire for a report wastes critical time that should go to alerting others, and asking a coworker's opinion delays the one action that actually needs to happen right away.

question: An employee smells gas near the building's utility room. What should she do first?

options.A: Leave the area immediately and report it from outside
options.B: Investigate the smell's source
options.C: Turn on the exhaust fan in the room
options.D: Text a coworker about the smell

explanation: A gas smell near a utility room is a serious hazard, so the first step is leaving the area immediately and reporting it from a safe distance, never staying near a possible gas leak to investigate. Turning on the exhaust fan or any other electrical switch near a suspected gas leak can create a spark and ignite the gas. Texting a coworker about it, instead of getting away and reporting it properly, wastes time that matters in a gas leak situation.

question: During a fire drill, an employee notices a coworker with a mobility impairment struggling to reach the stairwell because the elevators are locked out during drills, as required. What should the employee do?

options.A: Carry the coworker down the stairs quickly without waiting
options.B: Continue to the exit alone since drills aren't real emergencies
options.C: Stay with the coworker at the designated assistance area
options.D: Assume building facilities staff already know and will handle the situation

explanation: The right response is to stay with the coworker and use the designated evacuation chair or assistance area set up for exactly this situation, since mobility-impaired evacuation procedures exist for real emergencies as well as drills. Physically carrying a coworker down stairs risks injury to both people and bypasses the equipment and procedure meant for this. Treating a drill as not requiring a real, careful response defeats the purpose of practicing the procedure correctly. And assuming facilities staff already know and will handle it leaves the coworker unassisted based on an assumption nobody has confirmed.

question: A caterer is planning a 200-guest wedding event three months out. What should she identify first as a project resource need?

options.A: The guest list seating chart
options.B: A detailed hour-by-hour plan for the entire event day
options.C: The venue's parking capacity
options.D: The staff, equipment, and ingredients needed

explanation: The first project-resource question for a large catering event is what staff, equipment, and ingredients it will require, since those drive nearly every other planning decision. A seating chart matters, but it's a guest-management detail, not a resource-planning starting point. A detailed hour-by-hour schedule comes later, once the resource needs are known, and parking capacity is a venue logistics detail rather than the caterer's own resource requirement.

question: A small tech company is scoping a new internal software tool. Early planning identifies the need for two developers, a designer, and a $15,000 software-licensing budget, but nobody has assigned a project timeline. What resource-identification gap does this reveal?

options.A: Time itself was not identified and planned for as a project resource
options.B: The company never identified a sponsor to approve the licensing budget itself
options.C: The two developers may not have the right skills
options.D: The designer's role was never clearly defined

explanation: Identifying people, a designer, and a budget but never assigning a timeline shows that time itself was overlooked as a project resource that has to be planned for just like staff or money. The scenario does describe a budget already set, which implies someone approved it, so a missing sponsor isn't the gap the scenario points to. Nothing in the scenario suggests the developers lack the right skills, and while role clarity matters, the specific gap described is the missing timeline, not the designer's job description.

question: A small bakery wants to catch inconsistent cookie sizes before they reach customers. Which quality-control measure addresses this directly?

options.A: Hiring a new head baker
options.B: Asking customers to fill out a survey after buying
options.C: Raising the price of each cookie
options.D: Weighing dough portions before each bake

explanation: Weighing a sample of dough portions before baking directly catches size inconsistency at its source, before the cookies ever reach a customer. Hiring a new head baker doesn't guarantee more consistent portioning on its own. A post-purchase satisfaction survey only reveals problems after customers have already received inconsistent cookies, and raising the price has nothing to do with catching a sizing problem.

question: A furniture workshop wants to catch defective chair joints before shipping finished pieces to customers. Which measure addresses this directly?

options.A: Offering a longer warranty period
options.B: Hiring more retail sales staff
options.C: Lowering the shipping price
options.D: Inspecting sample joints against a strength standard

explanation: Inspecting a sample of finished joints against a written strength standard catches defective joints before they ship, which is exactly the quality-control gap the workshop wants closed. A longer warranty only addresses defects after a customer already has a faulty chair. Hiring more sales staff and lowering the shipping price both affect the business side of the sale, not whether the joints themselves are actually sound.

question: A juice bottling plant fills thousands of bottles per shift and cannot test every single bottle for fill volume. What quality-control approach best fits this situation?

options.A: Testing just the first and last bottle of each shift
options.B: Manually inspecting every single bottle by eye, which slows the entire line
options.C: Relying on customer complaints to flag issues
options.D: Statistical sampling of bottles to estimate fill accuracy

explanation: Statistical sampling at regular intervals gives a reliable, practical estimate of fill accuracy across thousands of bottles without needing to test every single one, which fits a high-volume bottling line.
